User request: no file involved, just settling an argument at lunch - when people say a pdf is searchable versus scanned, whats actually different inside the file? i have to explain it to a coworker tomorrow

content.text:
Short answer
- “Scanned PDF” usually means each page is just an image (a bitmap) embedded in the PDF. There’s no real text inside to select or search.
- “Searchable PDF” means the PDF contains actual text objects (a text layer) that search engines and the viewer can index and you can select/copy. That text can be original digital text (born‑digital) or text produced by OCR placed over a scanned image.

What’s actually different inside the file
- Scanned (image-only) PDF
  - Each page contains an image XObject (JPEG, PNG, JBIG2, etc.).
  - No text drawing operators (BT/ET, Tj/TJ) that represent characters.
  - No font or ToUnicode mapping for the page content.
  - Result: you cannot select, copy, or reliably search for words.

- Searchable PDF (two subcases)
  - Born‑digital searchable PDF:
    - Pages contain text drawing commands (operators that place glyphs) and embedded fonts with ToUnicode maps.
    - Text is “real” vector/text content produced by the application that created the PDF.
  - Scanned + OCR (image + text layer):
    - The page still has the scanned image, but the PDF also contains an invisible/overlay text layer with text objects positioned to match the image.
    - The overlay text is what search/copy uses; visually you still see the image.
    - The text may be imperfect if OCR made mistakes.

Practical effects and extra notes
- Search/select/copy: only possible if there’s a text layer or real text objects.
- File size: image-only PDFs can be large; OCR doesn’t necessarily reduce size (but images can be compressed).
- Copy/paste quality: OCR-generated text can contain errors, wrong spacing, or wrong Unicode mapping; born-digital text is usually clean.
- Accessibility: searchable text helps screen readers, but true accessibility prefers tagged PDFs and semantic structure, not just a text layer.
- Verification methods:
  - Try selecting text in a PDF viewer. If you can select words, there’s a text layer.
  - Check Document Properties → Fonts: if fonts are listed the file has text objects.
  - Use an OCR tool: if the reader offers “Recognize Text,” it will add a text layer to image-only PDFs.

Short example you can say at lunch
- “If a PDF is ‘scanned’ it’s usually just pictures of pages. If it’s ‘searchable’ it contains real text—either originally created as text or added by OCR—so you can search, select, and copy words.”
